newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economy could fall into recession - institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economy could fall into recession - institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economic activity is continuing a downward trend established at the end of 1996 that could lead to a long recession, the Belgrade-based Market Research Institute (IZIT) said on Tuesday.

"Economic activity definitely changed direction and instead of strengthening, it shows obvious weakening," said Tomislav Milisavljevic, the institute's leading economist, while presenting IZIT's latest monthly report.
"This is a serious warning that our economy can get into a long and uncertain recession," he told reporters.
Economic trends that were recently pointing up turned decisively down, causing serious deterioration in the business climate.
About 44 percent of industries polled saw the business climate as very unfavourable, an increase of nine percentage points over a month ago, the report said.

Lack of working capital and financial discipline, insolvency, low purchasing power and capacity utilisation, labour surplus and enormous fiscal burden were the main reasons for the choking business activity.

December retail prices gained 4.4 percent after a 1.8-percent rise the previous month, but December industrial production continued declining.December production shed two percent from the previous month, and November fell 7.2 percent from October.
Meanwhile, December producer prices jumped 6.3 percent after a 1.2-percent increase in November.
Exports and imports also fared poorly in December. Exports stood at $167.5 million, down 13.3 percent on November, and imports fell 6.6 percent to $396 million.
Total 1996 imports stood at $4.102 billion, up 53.9 percent over 1995, but exports gained only about 20 percent to $1.842 billion.

Export orders declined in Janaury to post the the third consecutive monthly drop. Thirty percent of surveyed firms, up from 25 percent in the previous month, said they had smaller export orders. Only 24 percent said their export orders increased at beginning of January.
IZIT's analysts said the political crisis, which erupted after annulment of opposition victories in the November 17 local elections, added to businesses' difficulties.
"The political situation in December was extremely unfavourable,and it will have a long-term effect on the country's economy," IZIT general manager Jovan Todorovic said.

"The international environment is more unfavourable today then it was yesterday," he said, adding that Yugoslavia was further estranged from international financial institutions, funds and markets than it was a year ago.
According to some estimates, the country needs about $2 billion in fresh funds to keep the economy going at last year's pace.
"Without external funds,it will be difficult to repeat the 1996 performance," Milisavljevic said.
